_about: The dashboard To-Do feed. Refreshed at every Rule 9 checkpoint alongside the session handoff — this is the handoff distilled into plain language for the 📋 button on every tab. Split For Sam (curation / decisions only a human makes) and For Fable (engineering, the next session picks up).
_session: SkyTouch (2026-09-10) — the rest of the phantoms, and three guards that reported nothing
_status: The dark-mode work is now through all four kinds of fault that a person reading the code cannot see: color names that were never defined, white backgrounds hard-coded as panels, white text sitting on a colored button whose color flips, and two tabs that kept their own private light/dark switch. Forty-seven color names and eighty-eight places in total. Mobile is clean on every tab at phone width, and a test now guards it. What is left is ordinary and individually named by the accessibility sweep. Three questions are waiting on Sam, and all three are the same shape: the fix is correct but it changes how things look in normal light mode, so it is a design call rather than a repair. Separately, three checks that were supposed to be protecting us turned out to be reporting nothing at all — one because the daily robot's own commits never run the tests, one because the test file was never wired to anything, and one because it was written so it could never fail. All three are fixed.

items.text: A real bug found while doing the dark-mode work, and it is not a dark-mode bug — it is wrong in both light and dark. Twenty-four places in the code ask for a color by a name that was never defined and give no backup, which browsers treat as 'skip this line entirely'. On the College Briefing tab that means the progress bar inside the briefing draws nothing at all and two accent borders never appear. Fixing it is straightforward, but it changes how the tab looks in normal light mode too, so it is yours to say whether those bars and borders should start showing.

A method note for whoever picks the theme work back up. This run fixed 62 places where a color name fell through to a hard-coded light value in dark mode, and the accessibility sweep's score did not move at all — because none of those 62 places is on screen when the sweep runs. They live in panels the page only builds when you click into them. So do not judge a color-token fix by the sweep's number: open the page in both themes and read the color names off the page directly. That check is written down in the lane file.

The moment MAP restores the six CPL lifecycle checks, put them back in the daily fetch — it is one line, and the funding model's counselor-accepted measure starts publishing again with no other change. They were removed on MAP's side around 8 September, which is what took the dashboard down for three days; we stopped asking for them so the rest of the data could flow. The schema probe (Actions, Discover MAP datasets) still watches all six every run, so it will say when they are back.

The daily history file stops at 7 September because the dashboard did not run for three days. Once a fresh run lands, fill in 8 and 9 September as interpolated entries and mark them as such — otherwise the dashboard's one-day change figure silently compares against a date three days back. Cannot be done before the new run exists: interpolation needs both ends.

The dashboard builder reads MAP columns by name but falls back to a guessed POSITION when the name is missing, in 51 places. Those positions were written when one report had 25 columns; it now has 19, so the guess points past the end of the row and crashes. That is exactly what took the cron down. One was fixed where it crashed; the other 50 are the same hazard waiting. Each should either read by name only, or say plainly that it cannot find the column.

You asked that a course carrying a C-ID or CCN designation take its description from the statewide template rather than from the colleges. We cannot do that yet: MAP holds the designation itself but not the wording that goes with it, on 541 courses (484 C-ID and 57 CCN). Those cards now say so plainly — they name the statewide descriptor as the authority and note that MAP does not hold its text — instead of presenting a consolidation as if it were the official wording. The question for you is whether ASCCC publishes the descriptor text in a form we can load, and who to ask. Once we have it, using it is a small change.

Sam described what CPL mode should be, and it is not the current one. Instead of course circles renamed after credentials, he wants a second map whose entities are the exhibits themselves — a Firefighter 1 exhibit shown the way a course is shown, with each college's local version of it as a member underneath, grouped into disciplines, and a ring around any exhibit that courses have been articulated to. This needs a new data build: the file we have runs course-to-credential, which is the opposite direction. His exact words are recorded in the SkyView lane notes. It is a sizeable piece of work, not a session's tidy-up.

On a phone the sky opens wide enough that discipline names get cut off at both edges of the screen. Narrowing the opening view would fix it, but how wide the sky is also decides whether each discipline's individual courses are drawn at all — open it too narrow on a small screen and some disciplines lose their stars. It needs your eye rather than a measurement, because every number we have was taken on a machine that is not yours.

A small housekeeping one, not blocking anything. The new SkyView question surface is registered everywhere in the code, but the live database rule that lists which surfaces a Sierra instruction can be scoped to has not been widened to include it. It only matters the day you want to write an instruction that applies to SkyView questions and nothing else. Say the word and it is a one-line change.

Seven test files print no readable count of what they checked, so if their checks quietly vanished nothing would notice. The build says so on every run and nobody has claimed it. This is the same failure that hid three real problems this session: a check that cannot fail looks exactly like a check that passed.

Your ruling on where skill statements come from unblocked the course outline's skills layer — published agency standards are the text of record, an ACE exhibit fills a gap they leave, the MAP team overrides either, and a genuine conflict shows both side by side. But we hold none of that text: of 1,987 credentials classified, 64 of them welding, not one carries a skill field. So this is now a fetching problem, not a decision. The question for you is which published standard to start with — an AWS welding certification is the natural pilot.

You asked for a magic phrase people type before they can move a course, shifting to a team phrase later. That would be the first time anything is written from the map, which today writes nothing at all — so it goes through Governance and the privacy review before it ships rather than after. DR-24 now carries your name as its owner; say the word and the phrase gets scoped.

DR-24 is a governance row with an owner and no surface yet: an added skill lands as proposed with the reviewer's name and the day, and joins the published outline when a second curator agrees; a removal works the same way in reverse. Building that means the map's first write, so it routes through Governance and the privacy review first.

Two housekeeping items behind the CPL face. Fifty-five exhibits in the articulation crosswalk are no longer in today's MAP feed; they stay on the map flagged in words rather than dropped, and the fix is a re-seed of the crosswalk from a fresh custom report. And the credit-funnel numbers the face carries for context were read by hand on 2026-09-07; refresh them after the next custom-report load.

One call left over from the funding text sheet. The public explainer's footer holds two different things in one block: where the numbers come from, and the line saying this is a working model for discussion and not adopted policy. Section hiding now works everywhere else on that page, but the footer is deliberately excluded, because hiding the disclaimer would be the wrong outcome. Say whether you want the sources paragraph split off so it can be hidden on its own, and the disclaimer left always visible.

Sam's rule that expended and allocated are not interchangeable — colleges spend, the Chancellor's Office allocates — was applied at the one place it was found in the memo builder. The rest of the memo and report text has not been read against it. Check who the subject is in each sentence before changing either word; a blanket sweep would get it backwards.

A test guarding a phrase this run deleted kept passing while measuring nothing, because it asserted at most one occurrence and zero satisfies that. It is fixed, but it is the third time a test tied to exact wording has broken on correct work, and this was the first found by accident rather than by looking. Worth one pass over the suites for other at-most-N assertions whose subject could legitimately vanish.

Six tabs paint their panels in slightly different pale tints — a blue-grey on Team & RACI, a cream on the sign-in gate, a plain grey on Budget — because each one was written with its own color rather than a shared name. In dark mode they all now go to one dark panel, correctly. The question is only about LIGHT: should they also become one shared tint, or keep the six they have? Making them one is a look change across six tabs, not a fix, so it is yours to call. Nothing is broken either way.

About a dozen small grey notes on the Implementation Funding tab — the source line under the title, the notes under the cards, the goal citations, the footer — use the palette's faintest grey. It is meant for decoration, not for text you are supposed to read, and it falls below the accessibility floor in dark mode. Moving them one step darker fixes that, but it also darkens them on the light tab you have been working in, so it is your call rather than a silent fix.

The dark-mode faults left are dark greys sitting on dark backgrounds, and a handful of pale backgrounds that stay pale in dark mode — mostly on Credential Reference, Common Subjects and Budget. The accessibility sweep names each one individually, so fix exactly what it names rather than sweeping by color, which has produced a wrong list every time it has been tried. Separately, printing a page while COBI is in dark mode still comes out dark-on-dark in places: the masthead is fixed, the rest needs its own pass.

The automated check that runs after we deploy the shared assistant is failing, and it is the check that is wrong rather than the assistant. It asks whether the answer about the Los Angeles district happens to spell out two particular college names out of nine. The assistant is answering well — it says there are nine colleges, then names five of them with the right coordinators and figures — it simply chooses a different five each time. The script's own notes already predicted this and name the fix: ask whether the district roster was looked up, instead of whether the prose contains a particular name. A previous check was moved this way for the same reason. One small change, and it needs your go because it is a production check.

A quiet one worth knowing about before it bites. Los Angeles Pierce College is recorded under the spellings 'LA PIERCE' and 'LA Pierce', but not under its own name, 'Pierce College'. Every internal table spells it the long way today, so nothing is broken right now. If a file ever arrives from outside using the college's own name, it would match nothing and the college would simply be absent, with no error to notice. Adding the third spelling now costs nothing.
